Definition 3.3 --- Onto Function (Surjective)
content:
A function $f: A \rightarrow B$ is \textbf{onto} (or \textit{surjective}) if
every element of $B$ is the image of at least one element of $A$:
\[
    f \text{ is surjective} \iff
    \forall b \in B,\; \exists a \in A \text{ such that } f(a) = b
\]

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faInfoCircle\ Key Points:}}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item The \textbf{range equals the codomain}: $\text{range}(f) = B$.
    \item \textbf{To prove surjective:} for an arbitrary $b \in B$,
          find (construct) an $a \in A$ with $f(a) = b$.
    \item \textbf{To disprove:} find a $b \in B$ with no preimage in $A$.
    \item Requires $|A| \geq |B|$ for a finite surjective function to exist.
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.5cm}

title: Definition 3.4 --- Into Function
content:
A function $f: A \rightarrow B$ is called an \textbf{into} function if it is
\textbf{not onto}, i.e., there exists at least one element $b \in B$ that is
\textbf{not} in the range of $f$:
\[
    \text{range}(f) \subsetneq B
    \quad (\text{range is a proper subset of codomain})
\]

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textcolor{accentorange}{\textbf{Note:}} Every function is either onto or into.
``Into'' simply means the function does not cover the entire codomain.
\textit{(Past Paper 2025 Q3 directly asks to describe and give examples of
one-to-one, onto, into, and bijective functions.)}

\vspace{0.5cm}

title: Definition 3.5 --- Bijective Function (One-to-One Correspondence)
Theorem 3.1 --- Bijection and Equal Cardinality
content:
For finite sets $A$ and $B$, a bijection $f: A \rightarrow B$ exists if and
only if $|A| = |B|$.

Moreover, for a function $f: A \rightarrow B$ with $|A| = |B|$:
\[
    f \text{ is injective} \iff f \text{ is surjective} \iff f \text{ is bijective}
\]

Definition 3.8 --- Inverse Function
content:
Let $f: A \rightarrow B$ be a \textbf{bijective} function. The \textbf{inverse}
of $f$, written $f^{-1}: B \rightarrow A$, is the unique function defined by:
\[
    f^{-1}(b) = a \iff f(a) = b
\]

\vspace{0.3cm}
Equivalently, $f^{-1}$ satisfies:
\[
    f^{-1} \circ f = I_A \qquad \text{and} \qquad f \circ f^{-1} = I_B
\]

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faInfoCircle\ Key Points:}}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item A function has an inverse \textbf{if and only if} it is bijective.
    \item $f^{-1}$ is obtained by \textbf{swapping} the roles of input and output.
    \item $(f^{-1})^{-1} = f$ --- the inverse of the inverse is the original.
    \item $(g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$ --- reverse order for compositions.
    \item \textbf{Do not confuse} $f^{-1}(x)$ (inverse function) with
          $[f(x)]^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{f(x)}$ (reciprocal).
\end{itemize}

Definition 3.11 --- Solving Recurrences by Iteration
content:
To solve $a_n = f(a_{n-1}, a_{n-2}, \ldots)$ by \textbf{iteration}:

\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{Step \arabic*:}, leftmargin=3.5em]
    \item \textbf{Expand} the recurrence repeatedly:
          $a_n \to a_{n-1} \to \cdots \to a_0$.
    \item \textbf{Identify} the pattern after $k$ expansions.
    \item \textbf{Substitute} $k = n$ to get the closed form.
    \item \textbf{Verify} the closed form satisfies the original recurrence
          and initial conditions.
\end{enumerate}

Definition 3.12 --- Big-O Notation
content:
Let $f$ and $g$ be functions from $\mathbb{Z}^+$ (or $\mathbb{R}^+$) to $\mathbb{R}$.
We say $f(n)$ is \textbf{Big-O of $g(n)$}, written $f(n) = O(g(n))$, if there exist
positive constants $C$ and $k$ such that:
\[
    |f(n)| \leq C \cdot |g(n)| \quad \text{for all } n > k
\]

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faInfoCircle\ Key Points:}}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item $C$ is called the \textbf{witness constant} and $k$ is the
          \textbf{threshold}. We only need these to exist --- we do not need
          the smallest possible values.
    \item $f(n) = O(g(n))$ means $f$ grows \textbf{no faster} than $g$
          (up to a constant factor) for large $n$.
    \item Big-O gives an \textbf{upper bound} on the growth rate of $f$.
    \item We always choose the \textbf{simplest} and \textbf{tightest}
          Big-O expression: e.g.\ prefer $O(n)$ over $O(n^2)$ if both hold.
    \item \textbf{Drop lower-order terms} and \textbf{constant coefficients}:
          $7n^3 + 5n^2 + 100 = O(n^3)$.
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.5cm}

title: Definition 3.13 --- Big-$\Omega$ and Big-$\Theta$ Notation
content:
\textbf{Big-$\Omega$ (lower bound):} $f(n) = \Omega(g(n))$ if there exist positive
constants $C$ and $k$ such that:
\[
    |f(n)| \geq C \cdot |g(n)| \quad \text{for all } n > k
\]
$f$ grows \textbf{at least as fast} as $g$.

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textbf{Big-$\Theta$ (tight bound):} $f(n) = \Theta(g(n))$ if
$f(n) = O(g(n))$ \textbf{and} $f(n) = \Omega(g(n))$, i.e.\ there exist
positive constants $C_1$, $C_2$, and $k$ such that:
\[
    C_1 \cdot |g(n)| \leq |f(n)| \leq C_2 \cdot |g(n)| \quad \text{for all } n > k
\]
$f$ and $g$ have \textbf{exactly the same} growth rate (up to constants).

\vspace{0.4cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|c|l|l|}
\hline
\rowcolor{primaryblue!20}
\textbf{Notation} & \textbf{Meaning} & \textbf{Bound Type} \\
\hline
$O(g)$ & $f$ grows at most as fast as $g$ & Upper bound \\
\hline
$\Omega(g)$ & $f$ grows at least as fast as $g$ & Lower bound \\
\hline
$\Theta(g)$ & $f$ and $g$ grow at the same rate & Tight bound \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.5cm}

title: Theorem 3.3 --- Growth Rate Hierarchy
content:
The following ordering holds for large $n$ (each class grows strictly faster
than the previous):
\[
    O(1) \;\subset\; O(\log n) \;\subset\; O(n) \;\subset\; O(n \log n)
    \;\subset\; O(n^2) \;\subset\; O(n^3) \;\subset\; O(2^n) \;\subset\; O(n!)
\]

\vspace{0.3cm}
If $f(n) = O(g(n))$ and $g(n) = O(h(n))$, then $f(n) = O(h(n))$ (transitivity).

Also: if $f_1(n) = O(g_1(n))$ and $f_2(n) = O(g_2(n))$, then:
\[
    f_1(n) + f_2(n) = O(\max(g_1(n),\, g_2(n)))
\]
\[
    f_1(n) \cdot f_2(n) = O(g_1(n) \cdot g_2(n))
\]

\vspace{0.5cm}

title: Example 1: Proving Big-O from the Definition
Example 2: Showing $n^2$ is NOT $O(n)$ --- Past Paper 2020 Q5(a)
content:
Show that $f(n) = n^2$ is \textbf{not} $O(n)$.

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{Solution:}}

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textbf{Proof by contradiction} (see also Section 1.6, Example 8):

Assume for contradiction that $n^2 = O(n)$. Then there exist positive constants
$C$ and $k$ such that for all $n > k$:
\[
    n^2 \leq C \cdot n
\]
Dividing both sides by $n$ (valid since $n > 0$):
\[
    n \leq C \quad \text{for all } n > k
\]
But this is impossible --- $n$ grows without bound and cannot be bounded above
by any constant $C$. For example, choose $n = \lfloor C \rfloor + k + 1$;
then $n > k$ yet $n > C$, giving a contradiction.

\textcolor{darkgreen}{\textbf{Conclusion:}} $n^2 \neq O(n)$. \qed

\vspace{0.5cm}

title: Example 3: Big-O of Polynomial and Logarithm
content:
Find the Big-O classification of each function. Provide witnesses $C$ and $k$.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), leftmargin=2em]
    \item $f(n) = 5n^3 + 3n^2 + 100$
    \item $f(n) = 2^n + n^{100}$
    \item $f(n) = \log_2(n^3) + n$
    \item $f(n) = (n+1)!$
\end{enumerate}

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{Solution:}}

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textbf{(a)} $f(n) = 5n^3 + 3n^2 + 100$

For $n \geq 10$: $n^2 \leq n^3$ and $100 \leq n^3$:
\[
    5n^3 + 3n^2 + 100 \leq 5n^3 + 3n^3 + n^3 = 9n^3
\]
Witnesses: $C = 9$, $k = 10$. \quad $\boxed{f(n) = O(n^3)}$

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textbf{(b)} $f(n) = 2^n + n^{100}$

For large $n$, exponentials dominate polynomials: $n^{100} \leq 2^n$ for $n \geq N$
(for some large $N$). So $2^n + n^{100} \leq 2 \cdot 2^n$.

Witnesses: $C = 2$, $k = N$. \quad $\boxed{f(n) = O(2^n)}$

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textbf{(c)} $f(n) = \log_2(n^3) + n = 3\log_2 n + n$

Since $\log_2 n \leq n$ for all $n \geq 1$: $3\log_2 n + n \leq 3n + n = 4n$.

Witnesses: $C = 4$, $k = 1$. \quad $\boxed{f(n) = O(n)}$

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textbf{(d)} $f(n) = (n+1)! = (n+1) \cdot n!$

$(n+1)! \leq (n+1) \cdot n! \leq n \cdot n!$ is wrong; note $(n+1)! = (n+1) \cdot n!$.
Since $n+1 \leq 2n$ for $n \geq 1$: $(n+1)! \leq 2n \cdot n!$.

\quad $\boxed{f(n) = O(n \cdot n!)}$

\vspace{0.2cm}
Or simply: $(n+1)! \leq (n+1)^{n+1}$ and grows faster than any $O(n^k)$ or $O(c^n)$,
so the tightest standard class is $O((n+1)!)$ itself.

\vspace{0.5cm}

Definition 3.14 --- Divisibility
content:
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $a \neq 0$. We say $a$ \textbf{divides} $b$,
written $a \mid b$, if there exists an integer $k$ such that:
\[
    b = a \cdot k
\]
We also say $b$ is \textbf{divisible by} $a$, or $a$ is a \textbf{factor} of $b$.
If $a$ does not divide $b$, we write $a \nmid b$.

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faInfoCircle\ Key Properties:}}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item $a \mid a$ for all $a \neq 0$ \quad (reflexive on $\mathbb{Z}^+$)
    \item If $a \mid b$ and $b \mid c$ then $a \mid c$ \quad (transitive)
    \item If $a \mid b$ and $a \mid c$ then $a \mid (bm + cn)$ for all $m,n \in \mathbb{Z}$
    \item $1 \mid b$ for all $b$; \quad $b \mid 0$ for all $b \neq 0$
    \item If $a \mid b$ and $b \mid a$ then $|a| = |b|$
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.5cm}

Definition 3.16 --- Modular Arithmetic
content:
For a positive integer $m$ called the \textbf{modulus}, integers $a$ and $b$
are \textbf{congruent modulo $m$}, written $a \equiv b \pmod{m}$, if $m \mid (a-b)$.

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textbf{Arithmetic operations modulo $m$:}
\[
    (a + b) \bmod m = ((a \bmod m) + (b \bmod m)) \bmod m
\]
\[
    (a \cdot b) \bmod m = ((a \bmod m) \cdot (b \bmod m)) \bmod m
\]
\[
    (a - b) \bmod m = ((a \bmod m) - (b \bmod m) + m) \bmod m
\]

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faInfoCircle\ Key Properties of Congruence:}}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item If $a \equiv b$ and $c \equiv d \pmod{m}$, then $a+c \equiv b+d \pmod{m}$
    \item If $a \equiv b$ and $c \equiv d \pmod{m}$, then $ac \equiv bd \pmod{m}$
    \item Congruence mod $m$ is an equivalence relation (proved in Section~2.4)
\end{itemize}

Theorem 3.4 --- Bézout's Identity
content:
For any integers $a$ and $b$ (not both zero), there exist integers $s$ and $t$
(called \textbf{Bézout coefficients}) such that:
\[
    \gcd(a,b) = sa + tb
\]
These coefficients can be found by the \textbf{extended Euclidean algorithm}.

Definition 3.20 --- Cryptography Terminology
content:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|}
\hline
\rowcolor{primaryblue!20}
\textbf{Term} & \textbf{Meaning} \\
\hline
\textbf{Plaintext}       & Original, readable message \\
\hline
\textbf{Ciphertext}      & Encrypted, unreadable message \\
\hline
\textbf{Encryption}      & Process of converting plaintext to ciphertext \\
\hline
\textbf{Decryption}      & Process of converting ciphertext back to plaintext \\
\hline
\textbf{Key}             & Secret value controlling encryption/decryption \\
\hline
\textbf{Cipher}          & Algorithm for encryption and decryption \\
\hline
\textbf{Cryptanalysis}   & Breaking a cipher without the key \\
\hline
\textbf{Symmetric key}   & Same key used for both encryption and decryption \\
\hline
\textbf{Public key}      & Two keys: one public (encrypt), one private (decrypt) \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textbf{Letter-to-Number Encoding:} In classical ciphers, letters are mapped to
numbers using $A = 0, B = 1, C = 2, \ldots, Z = 25$.
All arithmetic is performed modulo 26.

Theorem 3.5 --- RSA Correctness
content:
In the RSA scheme with $n = pq$, $\gcd(e,\phi(n))=1$, and $d = e^{-1}\bmod\phi(n)$,
decryption correctly recovers the plaintext:
\[
    (M^e)^d \equiv M \pmod{n} \quad \text{for all } M \text{ with } \gcd(M,n)=1
\]

    \item Decrypt \texttt{GXEVKZEX} with $k = 3$
    \item Decrypt \texttt{ZHOFRPH} with $k = 3$
\end{enumerate}

\vspace{0.2cm}


\item

title: Practice Problem 16
content:
For the affine cipher with keys $(a, b)$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), leftmargin=2em]
    \item Encrypt \texttt{LOGIC} using $a = 5$, $b = 8$.
    \item Decrypt \texttt{RCLLA} using $a = 5$, $b = 8$.
    \item Encrypt \texttt{MATH} using $a = 11$, $b = 7$.
    \item Why can we not use $a = 4$ in an affine cipher over $\mathbb{Z}_{26}$?
    \item Find the decryption key for $(a,b) = (9, 4)$.
\end{enumerate}

\vspace{0.2cm}


\item

title: Practice Problem 17
content:
Perform RSA key generation for each set of primes and encryption key.
Then encrypt the given plaintext and decrypt to verify.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), leftmargin=2em]
    \item $p = 3$, $q = 11$, $e = 7$; encrypt $M = 5$.
    \item $p = 5$, $q = 7$, $e = 5$; encrypt $M = 3$.
    \item $p = 11$, $q = 13$, $e = 7$; encrypt $M = 2$.
\end{enumerate}

\vspace{0.2cm}


\item

title: Practice Problem 18
content:
\textbf{Mixed function and cryptography:}
A message is encoded first using the affine cipher with $a=3$, $b=5$, then the
result is shifted by $k=4$ using the Caesar cipher.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), leftmargin=2em]
    \item Write the composed encryption formula as a single affine cipher.
    \item Encrypt \texttt{HELLO} using the composed cipher.
    \item Find the decryption formula for the composed cipher.
    \item Is the composition of two affine ciphers always affine? Justify.
\end{enumerate}

\vspace{0.2cm}


\item

title: Practice Problem 19
content:
\textbf{Comprehensive problem:}
A company uses the RSA system with public key $(n, e) = (33, 7)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), leftmargin=2em]
    \item Factor $n = 33$ to find primes $p$ and $q$.
    \item Compute $\phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1)$.
    \item Find the private key $d = e^{-1} \bmod \phi(n)$.
    \item Encrypt the messages $M = 2$, $M = 5$, and $M = 10$.
    \item Decrypt the ciphertext $C = 14$ to recover the original message.
    \item Why would it be insecure to use $n = 33$ in a real RSA system?
\end{enumerate}
